newsitem.title: HUNGARY: GROWTH CREATES TRADE TENSION IN CENTRAL EUROPE-THINK-TANK.
newsitem.headline: GROWTH CREATES TRADE TENSION IN CENTRAL EUROPE-THINK-TANK.

text.p: Stong economic growth in central and eastern Europe is likely to continue, but its pace will be slowed by recurring trade balance problems in the long term, Hungarian think-tank Penzugykutato Rt said on Wednesday.

"CEFTA (Central European Free Trade Agreement) countries are unlikely to post an average annual growth rate substantially above three percent," Penzugykutato analyst Arnold Ludanyi told a news conference.

According to some analysts, the gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by an average five percent annual rate in the region, bringing economic performance close to western European levels over the next 20 years, he added.

However, last year's record 10 billion rise in the total trade deficit of CEFTA to 24 billion showed that growth creates recurring tensions in the trade balance of these countries, Penzugykutato said.

Unfavourable foreign trade processes have triggered serious economic policy debates in the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Poland, the think-tank said in its new publication, introduced to the press at the news conference.
"In Poland, the overheating of the economy got into the focus, while in Slovakia and the Czech Republic exchange rate policies did," it said.

Other current account items almost offset Poland's trade deficit, while the Czech current account gap widened to the GDP's 7.6 percent in 1996 from 3.7 percent in 1995 and Slovakia turned a 2.2 percent surplus into a 1.5 percent gap, it said.

Each of the three countries is expected to restrict imports, the think-tank said, adding that they were likely to reduce money supply to the economy by raising central bank interest rates and obligatory reserve rates for banks.
But some analysts say that interest rate hikes would boost speculative capital inflow and appreciating the national currencies would create further growth of imports.
The analysts believe that devaluation cannot be avoided in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Penzugykutato said, adding that the Slovak and Czech governments rigidly oppose devaluation.
"According to analysts, a further increase in trade deficit cannot be avoided if Prague and Bratislava do not change their exchange rate regimes," Penzugykutato said.
The Hungarian analysts spoke after that the Czech crown was pushed to record lows last week by short-selling and the Czech central bank introduced measures to squeeze market liquidity.
Penzugykutato said Hungary's example showed that growth recreates similar foreign trade problems in the region, although the situation of individual countries is variant.

Hungary had to launch in 1995 a strict austerity programme, curbing household consumption and government expenditure, to cut the current account and budget deficits boosted by an increase in economic growth in 1994.
The austerity measures cooled the economy to almost stagnation in 1996, but they have created the fundamentals of sustainable growth, Penzugykutato said.

The GDP is likely to grow by more than two percent this year, and this will probably increase the foreign trade deficit to between 3.3 to 3.5 billion this year from 2.7 billion in 1996, but revenues from tourism and direct investment would preserve the current account's stability, the think-tank said.

The GDP is likely to grow by three to four percent annually after 1997 and cyclically recurring trade gap problems will probably compel the country to introduce restrictions from time to time, Penzugykutato said.
"But the amplitude of the swinging can be reduced," said analyst Zita Maria Petschnig.

Penzugykutato analysts added that Poland, Slovakia and the Czech Republic were unlikely to introduce measures to restrict household consumption substantially as household demand there did not have a crowding-out effect on investments.
The think-tank said that the most developed countries in the region -- the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia -- have begun a long march to catch up with the West.
But continued structural reforms in the fields of financial services and the continuation of privatisation remained essential, Penzugykutato said.
